senses.gloss:
liṅgasthala
(‘Śiva as infinite ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
In वीरशैविस्म् (the philosophy and religion of the लिङ्गायत सेच्त्), शिव (Brahman, God) is called ‘Sthala’, which means infinite space or the origin of च्रेअतिओन् and dissolution of the universe.
When शिव divides himself into two aspects—liṅga and aṅga—the former is known as ‘liṅgasthala’. It is actually he himself.
See ŚAIVISM and ṢAṬSTHALA-SIDDHĀNTA.

liṅga
(‘sign’)
------------------------------------------
This word is commonly used to indicate the famous emblem of शिव. See ŚIVALIṄGA for details.
How ज्ञान or empirical knowledge is acquired, is an important topic discussed in the Indian philosophical systems. These means of knowledge are called ‘pramāṇas’. Out of the several such प्रमाणस् normally accepted by these systems, अनुमान or inference is an important and universally accepted one. The term ‘liṅga’ is used as a part of this अनुमान.
A statement of अनुमान generally has three parts: साध्य (major term); पक्ष (minor term); sādhana or लिङ्ग or हेतु (middle term).
If smoke is seen on a yonder hill one can infer from this लिङ्ग or sign that there is fire there.
See also ANUMĀNA and PRAMĀṆAS.

liṅgaśarīra
------------------------------------------
The jīvātman or the bound सोउल् has three śarīras or bodies. They are: sthūla-śarīra (gross body); sūkṣma or लिङ्ग śarīra (subtle body) and कारणशरीर (causal body).
The sūkṣma or the लिङ्ग śarīra comprises sixteen parts and is directly responsible for पुनर्जन्म or transmi-gration.
The sixteen parts are: the five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (organs of knowledge like the eyes); the five कर्मेन्द्रियस् (organs of action like the hands); the five prāṇas (vital airs like प्राण and अपान) and the मिन्द् (including the बुद्धि or the intellect).

Liṅgapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस्, generally grouped under the all-comprehensive term ‘smṛtis,’ contain a lot of material useful to the common masses, to educate them both in the spiritual and in the secular fields.
The Liṅgapurāṇa, considered as an important work of the Śaiva cults, has been classified among the Mahāpurāṇas or the major पुराणस्. It might have been composed between A. D. 600 and 1000. The total number of verses as per the different editions varies from 6000 to 11,000. The book, as available now, is in two parts and has about 9000 verses, the number of chapters being 108 in the first part and 55 in the second.
A sanskrit commentary by गणेश Nātu (early part of the 19th century), Śivatoṣiṇī by name, has been printed.
The contents are variegated. See under PURĀṆAS.

liṅgadhāraṇa
(‘wearing the शिवलिङ्ग [on the body]’)
------------------------------------------
Vīraśaivas are also called ‘Liṅgāyatas’ since they wear the शिवलिङ्ग (a stone emblem of शिव encased in a small casket) on their body.
Liṅgadhāraṇa is a part of the cere-monies connected with दीक्षा or initiation. The गुरु worships the लिङ्ग first and then ties it round the neck of the initiate.
See also ŚAIVISM and VĪRAŚAIVAS.
